tagline: Through Henderson to the Green River, with a blues composer’s name.
intro: The W.C. Handy Blues Trail links the towns of Union, Henderson and Daviess counties, reaching Henderson on the Ohio River and crossing the Green River at Spottsville. US 60 carries much of the drive, with KY 56 at the Union County end and US 41A through part of Henderson. The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet records the 59.525-mile corridor as part of the Blues to Bluegrass Scenic Byway, designated January 29, 2004.

Its namesake’s Henderson connection began well before the scenic designation. W. C. Handy met Elizabeth Price while performing at a barbecue here in 1896; they married that July. Handy called himself the Father of the Blues, but his contribution lay in publishing and popularizing an existing musical form.

Driving from the Webster County line, follow the corridor through Givens and Boxville to Morganfield, then along US 60 through Waverly and Corydon to Henderson. Beyond Henderson, the route continues through Spottsville and Reed, then Newman and Stanley, ending at the Owensboro bypass junction.

moments.title: Corydon
moments.text: Corydon’s name arrived by way of a song and, before that, a Roman poem. John and William Dorsey settled the town in 1849. John’s wife, Patsy, named it for the hero of “Pastoral Elegy,” whose name came from a lovesick shepherd in Virgil’s Eclogues. The former coal town incorporated in 1867. US 60 serves as Main Street, connecting Corydon with Henderson to the northeast and Morganfield to the southwest.

moments.title: Henderson
moments.text: John James Audubon lived in Henderson from 1810 to 1819, running small businesses while pursuing his interest in birds. A century later, librarian Susan Towles supplied research connecting him to land selected for a state park in 1934. The Civilian Conservation Corps developed lakes, trails and roads; with Works Progress Administration help, it built the museum and other park buildings from local stone and millwork. The museum’s tower includes small niches for nesting birds, a detail that gives its subject a place in the building itself. Alice Tyler lent her family’s Audubon collection to the new museum, which opened in July 1938.

moments.title: Spottsville
moments.text: Two Spottsville bridges, built 91 years apart, shared a ribbon cutter. Irma Stanley Day cut the ribbon for the original Green River crossing in 1931 and for its replacement, completed in 2022. The old bridge’s narrow deck had led the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet to classify it as functionally obsolete in 2013; it was also structurally deficient. The crossing sits beside a longer history of river navigation: the community contains the Green River Lock & Dam and remains of locks replaced in the mid-1960s. US 60 forms Spottsville’s northern edge, while the Green River marks its eastern boundary.
